newsitem.title: UK: Oil markets up on U.S. stock expectations.
newsitem.headline: Oil markets up on U.S. stock expectations.

text.p: World oil markets gained ground late Tuesday on expectations of bullish weekly U.S. stock figures.

The weekly stock estimates from the American Petroleum Institute (API), due out late on Tuesday, are expected to show a draw in U.S. gasoline stocks of one to two million barrels for the week ended July 4.
For the same period American crude inventories were expected to drop by two to three million barrels.
Distillate stocks, comprising heating oil and diesel, were expected to build by one to 2.5 million barrels.
The world benchmark crude, North Sea Brent, was up 19 cents at $18.39 a barrel at the close.
Earlier on Tuesday prices had eased back on a bearish report from the International Energy Agency (IEA) and growing expectations of a resumption of Iraqi oil exports.

Thirsty U.S. markets guzzled more oil than expected this spring, helping to halt a dramatic slide in crude prices, but with inventories on the rise and Iraq close to resuming exports the reprieve will be brief, the IEA said on Tuesday.
News that talks between U.N. and Iraqi government officials are still continuing was slightly bullish.
Iraq's ambassador to the United Nations, Nizar Hamdoon, said Tuesday that U.N./Iraqi talks were continuing, though he couldn't say whether agreement on the key aid distribution plan was near.
"They are working out issues, both logistical and on political points," said Hamdoon. "But I am not aware of the outcome of today's meetings."
Ambassador Hamdoon said he was unaware of any major snags in the talks. He said he could not say when the distribution plan will be delivered to the U.N. secretary-general for approval.

Approval of the plan is necessary to allow the second round of Iraqi oil exports under the so-called oil-for-food deal which allows Iraq to sell up to $2.14 billion of oil over 180 days to buy and distribute aid under strict U.N. supervision.
Despite sporadic demand for oil products and prospects of temporarily tighter North Sea supply next month, many oil traders and analysts are bearish about prices over the next few months.
"While demand growth is expected to remain strong, its impact on oil prices may be offset by rising stock levels," said the Petroleum Finance Company (PFC).

"The final blow to prices however will be the rapid and concentrated resumption of Iraqi oil sales and the realisation of long-expected North Sea output hikes," said the PFC in its outlook for July to September.
The Asian market which has managed to prop up chronically weak Western markets this year is already beginning to show signs of faltering.
Last week Saudi Arabia slashed its crude prices to Asia where refinery profit margins have fallen to half their spring levels.

"No matter how European and U.S. demand fares this summer, the bullish price impact of another potential surge in Asian demand could be offset by the sheer size of the increase in crude production," said the PFC.
Also looming over the market is a German plan to sell about 7.3 million tonnes of crude from storage to help the country meet strict EMU borrowing requirements.
Last month Bonn said it would decide whether to proceed with the plan by July 11 when the cabinet is due to approve a supplementary budget.
But the IEA, which acts as the West's oil watchdog, frowned on the plan, calling it "unfortunate".
